intro: Send the same request to the Go / Gin and Python / FastAPI servers, one after the other, and compare how long each one takes.

math.title: Math calculation
math.description: Loops n times. Even indexes add 1, odd indexes add their last digit, and every iteration also adds a random number from 1 to 1,000.

generate.title: Data generation
generate.description: Builds n random users (id, name, gender, age), serialises them to JSON and saves the file on the server.

outOfRange: Enter a whole number between {{min}} and {{max}}.
slowWarning: Large values can take several minutes, especially on Python. You can cancel at any time.
similar: Both servers finished in about the same time.
comparisonUnavailable: No comparison available because at least one request failed.
timeVsNHint: Both axes are logarithmic. Run the same test with different n values to add points.

about.headline: Benchmark, compare, decide.
about.subheading: A real-time performance comparison of a compiled Go server and an interpreted Python server doing identical work.

go.description: Compiled, statically typed language with the Gin HTTP framework

python.description: Interpreted language with the modern, async-first FastAPI framework

tests.math: A CPU-bound loop with no I/O. It shows raw language speed: how fast each runtime can execute n iterations of simple arithmetic and random number generation.
tests.generate: Builds n user records in memory, encodes them as JSON and writes them to disk. It mixes CPU work (random data, serialisation) with file I/O.

notes.sequential: Requests run one after the other, Go first and then Python, so the two servers never compete for the same CPU.
notes.timing: Server execution time is measured inside each API and covers only the work itself. Round trip is measured by your browser and also includes the network and proxy.
notes.random: Each server draws its own random numbers, so the math result and the generated file contents differ between backends. Only the timings are comparable.
notes.language: Go compiles to machine code, while Python executes the loop step by step in its interpreter. The gap usually grows with n, which is why the chart axes are logarithmic.
